text.p: Germany's fourth and fifth largest commercial banks said on Monday they planned to merge, with the backing of insurance group Allianz AG, in a move set to change the shape of the German banking landscape.
Bayerische Vereinsbank AG and Bayerische Hypotheken- und Wechselbank AG said they were joining forces to form Bayerische Hypo- und Vereinsbank AG.
The new bank will be the second largest in the German banking market, after Deutsche Bank AG. The merger plans need to be approved by Germany's cartel office.

In the first step of a two-stage merger plan, shareholders in Hypo-Bank would be offered shares in Allianz AG at a rate of one Allianz share per six Hypo-Bank shares held, equating to a price of 75 marks per share on the basis of Friday's prices.

This would give Vereinsbank a stake of up to 45 percent in Hypo-Bank, with the Allianz shares involved coming from Vereinsbank's portfolio. An official offer document would be published next week, Vereinsbank said.
In a second stage, the full merger of the two banks would be prepared from October, with plans presented to shareholders for aproval by spring 1998 at the latest.
Allianz is a shareholder in both banks and will hold 15 percent of the new merged bank. The insurer said this would give it the benefit of an optimised network for sales of insurance and asset plans.

Allianz said nine percent of its capital, or about nine billion marks, would change hands in the deal. It warned that the switch could have an impact on its share price, but added that it would ultimately increase liquidity in the stock.

Bank shares in general surged on the Frankfurt bourse when computer trading opened. Vereinsbank shares jumped 12.2 percent to 92 marks while Hypo-Bank stock jumped 25 percent to trade just under the 75-mark offer price at 73 marks.
Investors' expectations that the German financial services sector was on the brink of a shake-up had gained fresh currency in recent weeks following news of a merger of two insurers under Munich Re.

Banking stocks had come back into favour in the two weeks since Munich Re said it would merge its two affiliates Victoria Holding AG and Hamburg-Mannheimer AG to form Germany's second largest primary insurer after Allianz AG.
"When things start to happen in the insurance sector the speculation spills over into bank stocks," Stefan Ermisch, banking analyst at Westdeutsche Landesbank said last week.
Yet top bankers had consistently dismissed the prospect of an early outbreak of mergers among private sector banks and say the public banks will be the first to consolidate.

Events over the last year appeared to confirm that view, with mergers mainly confined to state-owned regional banks, most notably Norddeutsche Landesbank and Bankgesellschaft Berlin AG which in May announced plans to merge.
Munich bankers and insurers had been expected to be at the heart of any reshaping of Germany's commercial banking market.

The rationale behind mergers is clear. Germany is regarded as heavily overbanked with more than 3,600 commercial, public and cooperative banks battling for market share, and a rate of one branch per 1,100 inhabitants.
The top five banks, led by Deutsche Bank AG, have a joint market share of just 14 percent and are struggling to make their costly retail branch networks more efficient.
The scenario announced on Monday was one of three possible scenarios for a revamp in the private sector.

The announced merger had long been mooted as a "Bavarian solution", sought by local politicians. But some analysts had warned that there could be little benefit in a merger of two banks that are relatively weak in investment banking.
The two banks, which will detail their plans at a news conference at 0900 GMT today, said the merger would cost around 1.3 billion marks in restructuring costs.
But it promised cost cuts of as much as one billion marks per year and said the joint group would have "markedly higher" earnings per share.
Sources said the two banks could cut between 5,000 and 7,000 jobs over the next five years.

Dresdner Bank AG, the number two bank in Germany, which could have merged with Hypo-Bank under one of the alternative scenarios, said in a statement that it did not expect the merger to disrupt its strategic links to Allianz.
